Description: explicit — no addProtocol on Native; Android serves app-supplied tile bytes another way
prompt: Android, Kotlin, MapLibre Native. Our vector tiles (MVT) sit in an encrypted blob on the device. I want the style JSON to reference them as `vault://tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}` and have my own code decrypt each tile and hand back the bytes. On the web I do this with `maplibregl.addProtocol`. Description: implicit — globe projection is in no MapLibre Native release
prompt: iOS, Swift, `MLNMapView`. Our style JSON has this at the top level: `"projection": {"type": "globe"}`. In the browser the same style renders as a globe; in the app the map stays flat however far I zoom out. I am on the newest MapLibre iOS from Swift Package Manager. What do I change to get the globe?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:**  
At the moment MapLibre Native (the iOS SDK you get from the Swift Package Manager) does **not** implement the `"projection": {"type":"globe"}` style key. The map will always stay in the Web-Mercator projection, no matter how far you zoom out. There is no setting you can flip in `MLNMapView` to make the globe appear.

**What you can do instead**

| Option | How it works | Pros | Cons |
|--------|--------------|------|------|
| **Leave the style as-is and accept a flat Mercator map** | Nothing to change in code; the style is parsed, the `"projection"` key is ignored. | No extra work, works on every iOS version. | No globe – the visual you see in the browser cannot be reproduced. |
| **Render the style in a Web View using MapLibre GL JS** | Load a `WKWebView` (or `SFSafariViewController`) that points to a small HTML page which creates a `maplibregl.Map` with the same style URL. | You get the exact same globe rendering that works in the browser. | You lose the native map view (no native gestures, no direct access to `MLNMapView` APIs). |
| **Wait for native globe support** | The feature is tracked in the native repo: **[#3161 – “globe projection on Native”](https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-native/issues/3161)**. When a release ships the support, you’ll just need to upgrade the SDK and the same style will work automatically. | No code changes when the feature lands. | You have to wait for the next native release (no ETA yet). |

---

### Why the globe doesn’t work on iOS today

* **MapLibre GL JS** implements the globe projection starting with version 4.0.0 (the style spec key `projection`).  
* **MapLibre Native** (both Android and iOS) reads the same style JSON, but the renderer has never had a globe implementation. The `"projection"` key is simply ignored, and the map stays in the default Mercator projection.  
* The missing feature is tracked as an open issue: **[#3161](https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-native/issues/3161)** – “globe projection on Native”. Until that issue is closed with a release note, there is no API or flag you can enable.

---

### How to keep your code ready for when globe support arrives

1. **Keep the `"projection"` entry in your style** – it will be a no-op now but will automatically take effect once the native SDK adds support.
2. **Upgrade the SDK** when a new version is released (watch the iOS changelog or the issue above). No code changes are required; the same style JSON will start rendering a globe.
3. If you need to detect at runtime whether the current SDK can render a globe (e.g., to hide a UI toggle), you can query the SDK version:

```swift
import MapLibre

let version = MLNVersionString()   // e.g. "7.0.0"
print("MapLibre iOS version: \(version)")

// No public API yet to ask “is globe supported?” – you have to rely on the version
// number that the changelog mentions when the feature lands.
```

When the changelog mentions “globe projection support added”, you can add a version check and enable any UI that toggles the globe.

---

### TL;DR

* **You cannot get a globe on iOS right now** – the native SDK simply does not support the `projection: globe` style key.
* **Work-arounds:** use a `WKWebView` with MapLibre GL JS, or stay with the flat Mercator map.
* **Future-proofing:** keep the projection key in your style and upgrade the SDK when issue #3161 is closed. No code changes will be needed at that point.

This is the web code I need to reproduce: `map.addSource('dem', {type: 'raster-dem', url: 'https://example.com/terrain.json'})` followed by `map.setTerrain({source: 'dem', exaggeration: 1.5})`. Description: implicit — interpolate-hcl drops the layer on Native before android-v13.7.1
prompt: One style JSON, shared between our web app (MapLibre GL JS) and our Android app (MapLibre Native, org.maplibre.gl:android-sdk 13.6.1). On Android this layer never draws, while every other layer in the style is fine and there is no crash: `{"id": "density", "type": "fill", "source": "tracts", "source-layer": "tracts", "paint": {"fill-color": ["interpolate-hcl", ["linear"], ["get", "density"], 0, "#f7fbff", 5000, "#08306b"]}}`. The same style is correct in the browser. Where do I look?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**What you’re seeing is the classic “layer is silently dropped because the paint expression can’t be parsed” symptom.**  

In MapLibre Native Android 13.6.1 the `interpolate-hcl` (and `interpolate-lab`) expressions are **not yet implemented**. When the style parser meets an unknown expression it discards the whole layer – no crash, no error dialog, just a log line like:

```
[ParseStyle] value must be a string
```

Because the layer is removed, the rest of the map renders fine and you only notice the missing fill.

### How to confirm it’s the expression

1. **Check the logcat output** while the map is loading. Look for a line that contains `ParseStyle` or `value must be a string` and mentions the layer id (`density`).  
2. **Temporarily replace the expression** with a plain `interpolate` (or a constant color) in the same style JSON and reload the map. If the layer appears, the problem is definitely the `interpolate-hcl` expression.

```json
"fill-color": [
  "interpolate", ["linear"], ["get", "density"],
  0,   "#f7fbff",
  5000, "#08306b"
]
```

If that works, you’ve isolated the cause.

### What to do on Android 13.6.1

| Option | What you need to change |
|--------|------------------------|
| **Upgrade the SDK** | `interpolate-hcl` (and `interpolate-lab`) were added in **android-v13.7.1** (see PR #4668). Bump your Gradle dependency to at least `13.7.1` (or any newer release) and rebuild. |
| **Stay on 13.6.1** | Replace the HCL-based ramp with a regular `interpolate` ramp that includes enough intermediate stops to approximate the HCL colour progression, e.g.:

```json
"fill-color": [
  "interpolate", ["linear"], ["get", "density"],
  0,    "#f7fbff",
  1250, "#c6dbef",
  2500, "#6baed6",
  3750, "#2171b5",
  5000, "#08306b"
]
```

   *Or* compute the HCL colours ahead of time (e.g. in a preprocessing step) and store them in a separate property, then use a normal `interpolate` on that property. |
| **Force-parse via raw JSON** | Android’s `Expression` builder does not expose `interpolate-hcl` yet, but you can still feed the raw JSON expression to the style (as you already do). It will only work once the runtime supports the operator, i.e. in ≥ 13.7.1. |

### Quick checklist for future parity issues

| Symptom | Likely missing feature | Minimum Native version that supports it |
|---------|------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| Custom URL scheme (`vault://…`) | `addProtocol` equivalent | No native support – use `ModuleProvider` or `CustomVectorSource` (Android ≥ 11.0.0) |
| Globe projection (`projection: "globe"`) | Globe rendering | Not supported in any release (open issue #3161) |
| 3D terrain (`map.setTerrain`) | Terrain rendering | Not supported (open issue #252) |
| `color-relief` layer | Elevation-based colour shading | Android 13.0.0, iOS 6.24.0 |
| `pmtiles://` URLs | Built-in PMTiles reader | Android 11.8.0, iOS 6.10.0 |
| `interpolate-hcl` / `interpolate-lab` | HCL/LAB colour interpolation | Android 13.7.1, iOS 7.0.0 |

### TL;DR for your case

* **Upgrade** your Android SDK to **13.7.1** (or newer) and the `density` layer will render exactly as it does in the browser.  
* If you cannot upgrade, **replace `interpolate-hcl` with a regular `interpolate` ramp** (or pre-compute the colours) and keep the style shared.

That’s the whole story – once the SDK version includes the expression, the layer will no longer be dropped. Happy mapping!

Description: explicit — color-relief exists on MapLibre Native
prompt: Android, MapLibre Native (Kotlin). I have Terrarium-encoded DEM tiles and I want elevation-banded color under my vector layers — green lowlands through brown to white peaks, with the breakpoints in the style so our cartographer can tune them. Can I do that in a MapLibre Android app, or do I have to pre-render colored raster tiles and ship those instead?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:**  
Yes – you can colour-code a Terrarium-encoded DEM directly in a MapLibre Android app.  
All you need is a **`raster-dem` source** that points at your Terrarium tiles and a **`color-relief` layer** that does the elevation-banded ramp. This works on any MapLibre Android release **≥ v13.0.0** (the version that introduced `color-relief`). If you are on an older release you must either upgrade or fall back to pre-rendered coloured rasters.

Below is a complete walk-through:

---

## 1. What the pieces are

| Piece | GL JS name | Native support (Android) | What it does |
|------|------------|--------------------------|--------------|
| DEM source | `raster-dem` | **v13.0.0+** (Terrarium & Mapbox-terrain-RGB) | Supplies elevation values to the style. |
| Colour-by-elevation layer | `color-relief` | **v13.0.0+** | Reads the DEM values (`["elevation"]`) and paints a raster colour based on an expression you define. |
| Optional shading | `hillshade` | any version | Gives a “shaded-relief” look on a flat map (does not raise the terrain). |

> **Note:** There is **no** `map.setTerrain()` on Native, so the map stays flat. The colour-relief raster is drawn on that flat map, exactly what you asked for.

---

## 2. DEM source – Terrarium encoding

The style JSON for a Terrarium DEM looks like this:

```json
{
  "id": "dem",
  "type": "raster-dem",
  "url": "https://example.com/tiles/terrarium/{z}/{x}/{y}.png",
  "tileSize": 256,
  "encoding": "terrarium",          // <-- important
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "minzoom": 0
}
```

* `encoding: "terrarium"` tells the renderer that the PNG stores elevation as the Terrarium format (R = elev/256 + 32, G = (elev % 256), B = 0).  
* The same JSON works on GL JS and on Native (v13.0.0+).  

If you are building the source from Kotlin instead of JSON, the same fields are available:

```kotlin
val demSource = RasterDemSource(
    id = "dem",
    url = "https://example.com/tiles/terrarium/{z}/{x}/{y}.png",
    tileSize = 256,
    encoding = RasterDemSource.Encoding.TERRARIUM,
    maxZoom = 14,
    minZoom = 0
)
style.addSource(demSource)
```

---

## 3. Colour-relief layer – the elevation-banded ramp

### 3.1. Style-JSON version (easiest to edit for a cartographer)

```json
{
  "id": "relief",
  "type": "color-relief",
  "source": "dem",
  "paint": {
    "color-relief-color": [
      "interpolate",
      ["linear"],               // or ["interpolate-hcl"] / ["interpolate-lab"] on v13.7.1+
      ["elevation"],            // the DEM value at the pixel
      0,   "#2e8b57",           // lowland – dark green
      500, "#6b8e23",           // gentle rise – olive
      1500, "#b8860b",          // mid-elevation – dark goldenrod
      2500, "#cd853f",          // sub-alpine – peru
      3500, "#d2b48c",          // alpine – tan
      4500, "#ffffff"           // peaks – white
    ]
  }
}
```

*All break-points (the numbers) are in **meters** because Terrarium stores metres.*  
Your cartographer can edit the numbers or colours directly in the style file – no code change required.

### 3.2. Adding / updating the layer from Kotlin

If you prefer to create the layer in code (or need to change the ramp at runtime), you can use `Expression.raw()` to feed the same JSON expression:

```kotlin
val reliefLayer = ColorReliefLayer("relief", "dem").apply {
    // The whole expression is written as a JSON string.
    // This avoids the missing Expression builder for interpolate-hcl/lab.
    setProperties(
        PropertyFactory.colorReliefColor(
            Expression.raw(
                """
                ["interpolate",
                 ["linear"],
                 ["elevation"],
                 0,   "#2e8b57",
                 500, "#6b8e23",
                 1500, "#b8860b",
                 2500, "#cd853f",
                 3500, "#d2b48c",
                 4500, "#ffffff"]
                """.trimIndent()
            )
        )
    )
}
style.addLayerBelow(reliefLayer, "water")   // put it under your vector layers
```

If you are on **android-v13.7.1+** you can also use the typed builder for `interpolateHcl` / `interpolateLab`, but the raw JSON works on every version that supports `color-relief`.

---

## 4. Optional: add a hillshade for “shaded relief”

```kotlin
val hillshade = HillshadeLayer("hillshade", "dem").apply {
    // default shading is fine; you can tweak the paint if you like
}
style.addLayerBelow(hillshade, "relief")   // hillshade under the colour-relief raster
```

The hillshade does **not** raise the terrain; it just adds a light-direction shading that makes the colour-relief look more three-dimensional.

---

## 5. Full Kotlin snippet (put it together)

```kotlin
mapView.getMapAsync { mapboxMap ->
    mapboxMap.getStyle { style ->

        // 1️⃣ DEM source (Terrarium)
        val demSource = RasterDemSource(
            id = "dem",
            url = "https://example.com/tiles/terrarium/{z}/{x}/{y}.png",
            tileSize = 256,
            encoding = RasterDemSource.Encoding.TERRARIUM,
            maxZoom = 14,
            minZoom = 0
        )
        style.addSource(demSource)

        // 2️⃣ Hillshade (optional)
        val hillshade = HillshadeLayer("hillshade", "dem")
        style.addLayerBelow(hillshade, "water")   // put it under the base map

        // 3️⃣ Colour-relief layer
        val relief = ColorReliefLayer("relief", "dem").apply {
            setProperties(
                PropertyFactory.colorReliefColor(
                    Expression.raw(
                        """
                        ["interpolate",
                         ["linear"],
                         ["elevation"],
                         0,   "#2e8b57",
                         500, "#6b8e23",
                         1500, "#b8860b",
                         2500, "#cd853f",
                         3500, "#d2b48c",
                         4500, "#ffffff"]
                        """.trimIndent()
                    )
                )
            )
        }
        // Place it **above** the hillshade but **below** your vector layers
        style.addLayerBelow(relief, "road-label")   // choose a layer that is on top of the base map
    }
}
```

*All of the above works on **android-v13.0.0** and later. If you are still on an older version, upgrade – the `color-relief` implementation was added in that release.*

---

## 6. What if you cannot upgrade?

| Situation | Work-around |
|-----------|-------------|
| **Running < v13.0.0** (no `color-relief`) | Pre-render the coloured raster tiles (e.g., with GDAL `gdaldem color-relief`) and serve them as a normal `raster` source. |
| **Need a custom colour ramp at runtime** | Keep the `color-relief` layer and update its `color-relief-color` paint property with `style.setStyleLayerProperty("relief", "color-relief-color", newExpression)` whenever the cartographer changes the breakpoints. |
| **Terrarium not recognized** (very old Native version) | Switch to Mapbox-terrain-RGB tiles (the same DEM encoded as RGB) – Native has always understood that format. |

---

## 7. TL;DR checklist for your app

1. **Use MapLibre Android v13.0.0 or newer** (the version that introduced `color-relief`).  
2. Add a **`raster-dem` source** with `encoding: "terrarium"`.  
3. Add a **`color-relief` layer** that references that source and defines the elevation-banded ramp in its `color-relief-color` paint property.  
4. (Optional) Add a **`hillshade` layer** for extra shading.  
5. Place the colour-relief layer **below** your vector layers so the vectors stay on top.  

If you meet those conditions, you **do not** need to pre-render coloured raster tiles – the native renderer will colour the DEM on-the-fly, and the breakpoints are fully editable in the style JSON (or via the runtime API).  

---  

**References from the skill**

* `color-relief` added in **android-v13.0.0** (see the skill table).  
* Terrarium support is part of the `raster-dem` spec and has been present since the early `raster-dem` implementation (no separate gap listed).  
* The example code mirrors the “Custom URL schemes” and “color-relief” sections of the skill.  

Feel free to ask if you need help wiring the layer order or exposing the ramp parameters to a UI for your cartographer!

Description: explicit — pmtiles:// is a built-in MapLibre Native scheme
prompt: iOS, Swift, MapLibre Native. Our basemap is one 3 GB `.pmtiles` archive on Cloudflare R2. On the web we register the PMTiles protocol with the `pmtiles` npm package and point the source at `pmtiles://https://...`. What is the iOS equivalent — do I need to stand up a tile server, convert the archive to MBTiles, or write a custom source?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:**  
You **do not** need a tile server, an MBTiles conversion, or a custom source.  
MapLibre iOS has native support for the `pmtiles://` scheme (since **iOS v6.10.0**).  
Just point the vector-tile source at the URL that you already use on the web:

```json
{
  "id": "basemap",
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "pmtiles://https://my-bucket.r2.cloudflarestorage.com/basemap.pmtiles"
}
```

Load the style normally in Swift, or create the source programmatically with the `URL` initializer (not the `configurationURLString:` initializer – see the iOS 17 trap below).

---

## 1. What you need on the iOS side

| Item | Requirement |
|------|--------------|
| **MapLibre iOS version** | ≥ 6.10.0 (the current stable release at the time of writing) |
| **Style JSON** | Must contain the `pmtiles://` URL (exactly the same string you use in GL JS) |
| **Swift code** | No custom source class is required. Use the regular `MLNVectorTileSource` (or let the style loader create it). |
| **Authentication** | If your R2 bucket is private, embed a signed URL or a token query-string in the URL – the same way you would for a normal `https://` tile source. |

---

## 2. Loading the style the “usual” way

```swift
import MapLibre

class MapViewController: UIViewController {

    var mapView: MapView!

    override func viewDidLoad() {
        super.viewDidLoad()

        // 1️⃣ Create the MapView
        mapView = MapView(frame: view.bounds)
        mapView.autoresizingMask = [.flexibleWidth, .flexibleHeight]
        view.addSubview(mapView)

        // 2️⃣ Load a style that already contains the pmtiles:// URL
        let styleURL = URL(string: "https://example.com/style.json")!
        mapView.mapboxMap.loadStyleURI(styleURL) { result in
            switch result {
            case .success:
                print("✅ Style loaded – PMTiles source is active")
            case .failure(let error):
                print("❌ Failed to load style: \(error)")
            }
        }
    }
}
```

If the style JSON already references the `pmtiles://` source, MapLibre will fetch the archive directly from Cloudflare R2, decompress the needed tiles on-the-fly, and render them. No extra code is needed.

---

## 3. Creating the source in code (optional)

Sometimes you want to add the source yourself instead of relying on the style JSON. Do **not** use the `configurationURLString:` initializer – on iOS 17 it mangles the `pmtiles://` scheme. Use the `URL`-based initializer instead:

```swift
import MapLibre

// 1️⃣ Build the URL (the same string you would use in the style)
let pmtilesURL = URL(string: "pmtiles://https://my-bucket.r2.cloudflarestorage.com/basemap.pmtiles")!

// 2️⃣ Create the vector-tile source
let basemapSource = MLNVectorTileSource(
    identifier: "basemap",
    configurationURL: pmtilesURL
)

// 3️⃣ Add the source to the style (after the style is loaded)
mapView.mapboxMap.style?.addSource(basemapSource)

// 4️⃣ Add a layer that uses the source (example: a fill layer)
let fillLayer = FillLayer(id: "land", source: "basemap")
fillLayer.sourceLayerIdentifier = "land"   // <-- name of the source-layer inside the PMTiles archive
mapView.mapboxMap.style?.addLayer(fillLayer)
```

**Why the `URL` initializer?**  
`MLNVectorTileSource(configurationURLString:)` internally runs `URL(string:)` on the string you give it. On iOS 17 the double-scheme (`pmtiles://https://…`) is interpreted as an invalid URL and the source fails to load. Passing a pre-constructed `URL` bypasses that bug.

---

## 4. Private R2 bucket / signed URLs

If the archive is not publicly readable, generate a **signed URL** (or add a token query parameter) that Cloudflare R2 will accept, and use that signed URL inside the `pmtiles://` wrapper:

```json
{
  "id": "basemap",
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "pmtiles://https://my-bucket.r2.cloudflarestorage.com/basemap.pmtiles?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256&X-Amz-Credential=…"
}
```

The signature is validated by R2 **before** the PMTiles reader touches the archive, so the same mechanism you use for ordinary `https://` tiles works here.

---

## 5. What to do if you are on an older iOS version

* **iOS < 6.10.0** – the built-in PMTiles reader does not exist.  
  *Upgrade the MapLibre SDK* (the latest 6.x series is compatible with iOS 12+).  
  If you cannot upgrade, the only alternatives are:
  1. Run a tiny tile-server that reads the PMTiles archive and serves standard XYZ tiles over HTTP, **or**
  2. Convert the archive to MBTiles (or a set of XYZ tiles) and serve those.

Both workarounds add latency and operational overhead, so they should be considered a last resort.

---

## 6. Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✅ | Use MapLibre iOS **≥ 6.10.0** |
| ✅ | Keep the `pmtiles://https://…` URL in your style JSON (or create a source with `URL(string:)`) |
| ✅ | No custom source class needed |
| ✅ | No external tile server required |
| ✅ | If the archive is private, embed a signed URL or token in the URL |
| ✅ | On iOS 17, avoid `configurationURLString:` – use the `URL` initializer |

---

### TL;DR code snippet (the most common pattern)

```swift
let styleURL = URL(string: "https://example.com/style.json")!   // style contains pmtiles://…
mapView.mapboxMap.loadStyleURI(styleURL) { result in
    // style (and the PMTiles source) is now live
}
```

That’s it – MapLibre iOS will download the 3 GB PMTiles archive from Cloudflare R2, cache the needed parts, and render the map exactly as it does in the browser. No server, no conversion, no custom source. Happy mapping!

Description: negative — registering a custom protocol in the browser
prompt: Browser app, MapLibre GL JS, TypeScript. I want to serve vector tiles out of an in-browser IndexedDB cache under a `cache://` scheme, so my style can reference `cache://tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}`. Show me how to register the protocol.
